summary.value: The paper addresses pervasive artifacts in LLM-agent benchmarks by proposing a component-wise taxonomy of issues across User, Environment, Evaluation System, and Ground Truth (Sec. 3.2; Table 3), covering problems such as ambiguous instructions, incorrect tool responses, brittle scoring, and erroneous ground-truth calls. Building on this taxonomy, the authors introduce AgentBenchCleaner, a three-stage automated pipeline: (1) rule-based filters for deterministic defects, (2) an LLM-as-a-judge for nuanced issues, and (3) an optional difficulty-based curation to increase challenge (Sec. 4; Figure 2). Applying Stages 1–2 yields an issue-cleaned benchmark; adding Stage 3 produces AgentHard-Bench, a harder derivative with standardized evaluation protocols (Sec. 4.3). Across six representative benchmarks (BFCL V3, ACEBench, DrafterBench, τ-Bench, τ2-Bench, CFB), the pipeline aligns well with expert judgments (F1 0.759–0.880; Table 4), removes large fractions of flawed or saturated tasks (e.g., 32.1% via issue filtering and 56.1% after the full pipeline; Sec. 5.3, Figure 5), and improves benchmark quality by reducing model agreement and increasing confidence-separation while preserving diversity (Table 4; Figure 4). The method also leads to clearer and more stable leaderboards—for example, τ-Bench rankings shift for 75% of models with widened top-model gaps (Table 5; Table 9). The authors will release the taxonomy, pipeline, and AgentHard-Bench to support robust and reproducible agent evaluation.

strengths.value:
1. Actionable, component-wise taxonomy. The four-component breakdown (User, Environment, Evaluation System, Ground Truth) is precise and operational (Sec. 3.2; Table 3), not merely descriptive. It pinpoints concrete, automatable failure modes such as “user role confusion,” “misleading tool design,” and “malformed tool calls,” with quantitative evidence on prevalence (e.g., τ-Bench shares in Table 2).

2. Taxonomy-to-pipeline mapping. The paper goes beyond auditing: it encodes the taxonomy into a practical three-stage pipeline that cleanly separates deterministic rule checks from semantic LLM judging and a final difficulty curation (Sec. 4.2; Figure 2). This modularity increases scalability and maintainability.

3. Carefully engineered judge prompting. The LLM-as-a-judge design is unusually thorough and transparent, including a generalizable template and a crucial “Actively Reconstruct the Conversation” rule to avoid false positives when milestone-only trajectories are provided (Appendix A.4). This is a notable methodological contribution for agent evaluation.

4. Strong, multi-pronged validation of issue detection. Human alignment is measured with both balanced subset labeling and full post-hoc verification (Sec. 5.2.1), achieving F1 0.759–0.880 (Table 4) and high end-to-end accuracy (Figure 3). This dual protocol convincingly supports the LLM-judge’s utility at scale.

5. Stage-wise ablations across six benchmarks. The paper quantifies each stage’s contribution to agreement, CI non-overlap, diversity, and compression (Tables 10–15), making the causal impact of rule filters, LLM judging, and difficulty-based curation clear rather than relying on end-to-end gains alone.

6. Cross-model robustness of the LLM judge. The judge works consistently across strong proprietary and open models (Gemini/Claude/DeepSeek), with comparable precision/recall per benchmark (Table 6). This reduces dependence on any single vendor and strengthens generality claims.

7. Measurable benchmark-quality improvements. After cleaning, separability improves in multiple ways—model agreement drops (e.g., ACEBench −0.138; τ-Bench −0.040) and CI non-overlap increases (e.g., ACEBench +0.181; τ2-Bench +0.050), while diversity is preserved or slightly improved (Table 4; Figure 4). The improvements are clearly contextualized against random-task baselines.

8. Practical leaderboard impact. The cleaned and harder versions materially change and clarify rankings (Table 5; Table 9; Figure 6): on τ-Bench, 75% of models shift, the top-2 swap, and the top gap widens from 0.018 to 0.045, demonstrating that artifact removal meaningfully affects conclusions practitioners would draw.

9. Compression with capability coverage safeguards. The pipeline achieves substantial compression (e.g., final 56.1% in Sec. 5.3; Figure 5) without hollowing out skills: embedding-based diversity remains stable (Table 4), subtask retention is analyzed in detail, and a 10% per-subtask floor protects breadth (A.7; Figures 7–8).

10. Breadth and depth of evidence across diverse benchmarks. The study spans six heterogeneous suites (Table 1), and the case studies cover all four components with concrete, real errors (Appendix A.1/Table 7)—e.g., τ-Bench “do-nothing” pass rate (38%), CFB mis-resolving “Melbourne,” DrafterBench’s incorrect system prompt—demonstrating the taxonomy’s wide applicability.

11. Support for dataset repair, not just filtering. The pipeline’s structured reasoning traces pinpoint minimal fixes (Appendix A.3), e.g., filename correction in BFCL V3 or enum mismatch in ACEBench, offering a practical path for benchmark maintainers beyond binary removal.

12. Clear scoping and usage guidance. The paper is explicit about when to use the issue-filtered set versus the difficulty-curated AgentHard-Bench and the dependence of Stage 3 on reference models (Sec. 6), which helps ensure fair downstream use.

13. Standardized evaluation protocol for the harder suite. AgentHard-Bench is positioned with “standardized evaluation protocols and explicit quality criteria” (Sec. 4.3), helping normalize practices across agent evaluations rather than proposing yet another idiosyncratic testbed.

weaknesses.value:
1. Residual error and brittleness of the LLM-as-a-judge undermines cleaning precision
- Evidence: F1 ranges 0.759–0.880 across suites (Table 4); post-hoc end-to-end accuracy is “at least about 77%” (Fig. 3). Failure modes include false positives from partial trajectories and “misjudgment of redundancy,” and false negatives on malformed/incorrect calls and incorrect tool responses (Sec. 5.5; App. A.2/Table 8).
- Why it matters: Systematic FP/FN directly affect which tasks are removed, potentially biasing the cleaned benchmark and downstream rankings.
- Actionable: (a) Report per-category precision/recall for the judge (e.g., by Table 3 categories) to identify weak spots. (b) Use judge ensembles with disagreement-based adjudication and calibrated thresholds to cap FP rates; measure cross-judge agreement (Cohen’s κ) beyond Table 6. (c) Add targeted counterfactual prompts for failure categories in App. A.2, especially “partial trajectory” and “redundancy” cases, and show error reductions. (d) Introduce light human-in-the-loop spot checks on high-uncertainty items to bound FP in the final release.

2. Rule-based filtering is assumed “perfectly aligned” without independent precision auditing
- Evidence: “Rule-based filtering is deterministic by construction and thus achieves perfect alignment” (Sec. 5.1). Fig. 3 reports proportions of rule-based TPs but does not quantify potential FPs.
- Why it matters: Determinism ≠ correctness; schema and policy rules can be over- or mis-specified, causing silent over-pruning.
- Actionable: Add a stratified human audit (by issue type and benchmark) of a random sample flagged by Stage 1; report precision with CIs. Publish the exact rule catalog mapping each taxonomy item (Table 3) to deterministic checks to enable external validation.

3. Difficulty-based curation (Stage 3) is under-specified and model-panel–dependent
- Evidence: Stage 3 is a “simple heuristic” that filters tasks “that nearly all models can solve” (Sec. 4.2), and its dependence on reference models is acknowledged as a limitation (Sec. 6). Thresholds and selection criteria are not fully detailed.
- Why it matters: Results and “hardness” may shift as model panels evolve, confounding longitudinal comparability and fairness across labs.
- Actionable: (a) Specify exact thresholds (e.g., pass-rate quantiles) and tie them to a fixed, versioned reference panel. (b) Provide sensitivity analyses showing how AgentHard-Bench composition and separability change under alternative panels. (c) Release a frozen “v1 reference panel” and a re-computation script so future users can reproduce/compare versions.

4. “More stable rankings” are not rigorously established
- Evidence: Stability is argued via lower agreement and higher CI non-overlap (Table 4; Fig. 4), while Table 5/9 emphasize ranking changes rather than test–retest stability.
- Why it matters: Stability should reflect robustness of ranks under resampling/noise, not just larger inter-model gaps.
- Actionable: Add bootstrap-based reliability: Kendall τ/Spearman ρ of rankings across many resampled task subsets (before vs after cleaning), plus Rank-Biased Overlap for top-k. Report indistinguishability counts with CIs (Table 9) and show reductions are statistically significant.

5. Diversity assessment is narrow and partly declines after curation
- Evidence: Diversity uses Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine distance (Sec. 5.1) and shows small drops on τ-Bench/τ2-Bench/DrafterBench (Table 4). Subtask retention plots (A.7, Figs. 7–8) are qualitative.
- Why it matters: Embedding distance may not reflect capability coverage; modest declines could accumulate with future updates.
- Actionable: (a) Complement with capability-aware metrics: subtask entropy, API-schema/type coverage, argument-shape diversity, and tool-graph structural diversity. (b) Quantify distribution shift (e.g., Hellinger distance) between original and cleaned sets per subtask and per component (User/Env/Eval/GT). (c) Report statistical tests to demonstrate that diversity losses are negligible.

6. Evaluation-system issues are in the taxonomy but not fully operationalized
- Evidence: “Evaluation System” issues appear in Table 3 (too lenient/too strict), yet the LLM-judge prompt omits evaluation issues “irrelevant to flaws in individual samples” (App. A.4), and Stage 1 examples focus on schemas/ground truth.
- Why it matters: Lenient harnesses (e.g., τ-Bench “do nothing” 38% pass; App. A.1) materially distort scores; lack of automated detection leaves an important artifact class under-addressed.
- Actionable: Implement harness-level detectors: (a) run standardized baselines (no-op, echo, random) to measure pass rates and flag tasks with inflated baseline success; (b) enforce semantic, execution-based equivalence instead of brittle string-match, and auto-flag high string/semantic mismatch rates; (c) publish per-benchmark evaluation-quality reports alongside cleaned tasks.

7. Lack of direct empirical comparison to prior curation pipelines
- Evidence: Related work contrasts MixEval/SMART/Arena-Hard conceptually (Sec. 2), but no side-by-side empirical comparison is shown.
- Why it matters: To substantiate the claimed advantages of a component-aligned, per-task filtering approach, it is useful to show superior alignment/separability vs baselines on the same inputs.
- Actionable: Reproduce MixEval/SMART-style filtering on the same base suites and compare: human alignment (Table 4 protocols), separability, diversity, and compression. Include a combined (“ours + SMART”) setting to demonstrate complementarity.

8. Limited reporting on scalability and cost
- Evidence: The pipeline claims scalability, but there is no accounting of cost/latency (Sec. 4–5). Judge robustness is shown (Table 6), not throughput.
- Why it matters: Adoption depends on predictable cost-quality trade-offs, especially for large suites (e.g., CFB 1,000 tasks; Table 11).
- Actionable: Provide end-to-end runtime and cost per 1k tasks for Stages 1–2, plus cost–quality curves (precision/recall vs budget via dynamic stopping or adaptive re-judging on uncertain cases).

9. Repair is demonstrated but not quantified or productized
- Evidence: App. A.3 gives three repairable cases and argues detectors “aid human-in-the-loop repair,” but no estimate of salvageable fraction or time-to-fix is provided.
- Why it matters: Filtering discards data; repair could recover coverage and diversity at modest cost.
- Actionable: Quantify a “salvage rate” by sampling pipeline-flagged items, estimating minimal-edit repairs and annotator time. Consider releasing a parallel “Repaired” subset with provenance tags.

10. Generalization beyond the six evaluated suites is claimed but not evidenced
- Evidence: The taxonomy is “easily applicable to unseen benchmarks” (Sec. 6), but experiments exclude large interactive suites like WebArena/OSWorld mentioned in Sec. 2.
- Why it matters: External validity strengthens claims of broad utility.
- Actionable: Add a small-scale pilot on one environment-rich suite (e.g., a subset of WebArena), reporting the same metrics (Table 4) to demonstrate portability.

11. Reproducibility gaps in pipeline specification
- Evidence: A representative judge prompt is provided (App. A.4), but complete rule sets, thresholds for Stage 3, and per-benchmark prompt variants are not fully enumerated.
- Why it matters: Without exact detectors and thresholds, reproducing Table 4–15 results is difficult.
- Actionable: Release (or include in the paper) the full mapping from taxonomy (Table 3) to rule detectors, all prompts per benchmark, and the precise Stage-3 thresholds/panel, along with seeds and evaluation harness configurations.

questions.value:
1. LLM-as-a-judge error analysis and mitigation
- Table 4 and Figure 3 show nontrivial judge errors (F1 0.759–0.880; end-to-end accuracy “at least about 77%”). Could you report per-category precision/recall aligned to the taxonomy in Table 3 (e.g., “Malformed tool calls” vs “Incorrect tool responses”) to localize weak spots?
- Appendix A.2/Table 8 lists recurrent FP/FN modes (“partial trajectory”, “misjudgment of redundancy”). Did you try prompt variants targeted at these modes? Please provide an ablation showing error reductions from such targeted instructions (citing Appendix A.4).
- Beyond Table 6, have you explored judge ensembles with disagreement-aware adjudication or calibrated thresholds to cap FPs? Reporting cross-judge agreement (e.g., Cohen’s κ) and the final decision rule would strengthen confidence.

2. Rule-based filtering validation
- Sec. 5.1 states “Rule-based filtering is deterministic … and thus achieves perfect alignment.” Determinism is not sufficient for correctness. Please add a stratified human audit of a random sample flagged by Stage 1 (by taxonomy category and benchmark) and report precision with confidence intervals. Also, could you publish the exact Stage-1 rule catalog mapping each Table 3 issue to concrete checks?

3. Stage 3 difficulty curation: thresholds, panel dependence, and sensitivity
- Sec. 4.2 (Stage 3) and Sec. 6 acknowledge dependence on the reference panel. What exact threshold defines “nearly all models can solve” (e.g., pass-rate ≥ p across the panel, required margin)? Please specify the versioned panel used.
- Provide sensitivity: how do AgentHard-Bench composition and separability (Table 4 metrics) change under alternative panels and thresholds? A small grid or bootstrap over model subsets would clarify robustness.
- Would you release a frozen “v1 reference panel” and script to re-compute curation for longitudinal comparability?

4. Ranking stability vs separability
- Claims of “more stable model rankings” (Abstract; Sec. 5.2.2) rely on agreement and CI non-overlap (Table 4) plus ranking changes (Table 5/Table 9; Fig. 6). Could you add bootstrap-based rank reliability (Kendall τ/Spearman ρ over many resampled task subsets) and top-k Rank-Biased Overlap before/after cleaning, with CIs, to directly quantify stability gains?

5. Diversity measurement and capability coverage
- Diversity uses Qwen3-Embedding-8B cosine distance (Sec. 5.1). To ensure capability coverage, could you add capability-aware metrics: subtask entropy, API/schema/type coverage, argument-shape diversity, and tool-graph structure diversity? Complement A.7 (Figs. 7–8) with quantitative distribution-shift measures (e.g., Hellinger distance) per subtask.
- Are the diversity findings robust to the choice of embedding model? A parallel analysis with a second embedding model would help.

6. Evaluation-harness issues: detection and remediation
- Table 3 includes “Too lenient/Too strict,” and τ-Bench’s “do-nothing” success (38%) is noted in Appendix A.1. Yet Appendix A.4 says evaluation issues were omitted from the judge prompt. Can you add harness-level detectors: (i) standardized baseline probes (no-op/echo/random) to flag inflated pass rates, (ii) semantic/execution-based equivalence metrics to identify brittle string matches, and (iii) per-benchmark evaluation-quality reports accompanying the cleaned sets?

7. Human labeling protocol details
- For the balanced subset validation (Sec. 5.1): how many experts annotated each benchmark, what were the instructions, and what was inter-annotator agreement? How were disagreements resolved? Please add CIs to the precision/recall in Table 4.

8. Exact definitions and computations of separability metrics
- Sec. 5.1 references “model agreement rates (Gupta et al., 2025)” and “CI non-overlap,” and Table 4 reports CI non-overlap “relative to baseline.” Please define the precise agreement formula (pairwise vs across-all), CI construction, number of random baselines, and the non-overlap computation. Sharing code would avoid ambiguity.

9. Comparison to prior filtering pipelines
- Sec. 2 argues conceptual complementarity to MixEval/SMART/Arena-Hard. Could you include side-by-side empirical comparisons on overlapping inputs: human alignment (Table 4 protocol), separability/diversity (Table 4), compression, and a combined (“ours + SMART”) setting to show additive gains?

10. Scalability and cost
- For adoption, please provide end-to-end runtime and cost per 1k tasks for Stages 1–2, broken down by benchmark size (e.g., CFB 1,000 tasks; Table 11). Include cost–quality trade-offs (precision/recall vs budget) via: (i) adaptive re-judging for high-uncertainty items, (ii) judge selection (Table 6) under a fixed budget.

11. Repairability and salvage rate
- Appendix A.3 shows three “minimal-fix” cases. Could you estimate a salvage rate by sampling pipeline-flagged items and reporting the fraction amenable to minimal edits, plus median annotator time? Would you release a parallel “Repaired” subset with provenance tags to balance compression with coverage?

12. Generalization beyond the six suites
- Sec. 2 mentions environment-rich suites (WebArena/OSWorld). A small pilot on one such suite—reporting the same Table 4 metrics—would strengthen claims that the taxonomy and pipeline generalize across interaction modalities.

13. Standardized protocol for AgentHard-Bench
- Sec. 4.3 claims “standardized evaluation protocols and explicit quality criteria.” Please enumerate these concretely: pass/fail semantics (tool-call vs final-state), allowed variances, and how they supersede inconsistent original harnesses. A compact “Eval Card” per benchmark would be valuable.

14. Reproducibility package
- Appendix A.4 provides a representative judge prompt for τ2-Bench. For full reproducibility, can you release: (i) all per-benchmark prompts, (ii) the Stage-1 rule library, (iii) Stage-3 thresholds and the exact model panel, (iv) seeds and harness configurations, and (v) scripts to compute metrics in Tables 4 and 10–15?

15. Retention safeguard and potential skew
- Sec. 5.3/A.7 use a 10% per-subtask retention floor. Why 10%? Please provide sensitivity showing how separability, diversity, and leaderboard conclusions change for 5%/15% floors, and whether the floor inadvertently preserves low-value subtasks.

16. Post-hoc validation specifics
- Figure 3 aggregates manual verification of pipeline-flagged tasks. Could you report per-benchmark and per-stage (Stage 1 vs Stage 2) FP rates with 95% CIs, and provide a confusion breakdown by Table 3 categories?

17. Clarify agent model panel and settings
- Table 5 lists many models with “thinking-on/off” variants. Were agent prompts, tool-calling scaffolds, and temperature identical across models? Did “thinking” modes change tool-use tendencies and thus Stage-3 curation? A short protocol table would help ensure comparability.

18. Quantify significance of heatmap improvements
- Figure 4 visually suggests reduced agreement for ACEBench post-cleaning. Please add quantitative tests (e.g., paired bootstrap on agreement statistics) to assess significance of changes beyond visual inspection.
